<reason>PRO built a clean core (coordination problem: parental controls exile the individual child; law shifts the default for the cohort) and defended it through every round. CON's strongest material was the asymmetry argument—liability drives platforms to universal ID checks in a way defaults do not—and the "who can still see them" reframe, both genuinely competitive. But PRO caught CON shifting between a minors-only regime (which needs the gate CON called catastrophic) and universal defaults (which still need to identify minors to prevent opt-out, as CON's own closing admitted), and CON never squarely answered the exiled-child point: "everyone gets the same safer product" doesn't help the child whose parents said no while the grade stays on the same platform. PRO's answers to pressure (reasonable-steps liability, advertiser-grade age inference, gambling/alcohol gates, decoy apps lack the network) were direct and grounded in ordinary knowledge. CON's closing misattributed its own B4.3 as a PRO concession, a small but real execution cost. Both sides had clipped turns. Clear but competitive PRO win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A2.1–A2.3 exposed the contradiction between CON's "verification is a privacy catastrophe" and "safer defaults for minors," forcing CON to migrate to universal defaults in B4.1; PRO then closed the loop in A4.6–A4.7 and A5.2 by showing that even universal defaults leave the grade on the same platform and still require identifying minors, while B4.4's asymmetry counter was the best CON answer but relied on an asserted, not demonstrated, inevitability of universal ID.</best_rebuttal>
